section_summary: This section combines State and Navy Department correspondence about proposals to restrict war-material and petroleum exports to Japan, including confidential reports that Japan was seeking greater oil supplies from the Dutch East Indies. It also contains correspondence and a detailed report from the American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression concerning fundraising, publicity, public opinion, lobbying, finances, and proposed embargo legislation. The final portion consists of internal State Department analyses concluding that ostensibly neutral export quotas would be transparently discriminatory, administratively burdensome, and less practical than direct restrictions on exports to Japan, supported by extensive trade tables for 1920–1938.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Warren R. Austin's embargo proposal
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Greene's letter forwarding Senator Warren R. Austin's proposal for an embargo on exports of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Joseph C. Green acknowledges receipt of Greene's May 3 letter and its enclosure from Senator Austin. The reply records the Department's appreciation without stating a position on the proposed embargo.

subfiles.title: Navy Department forwarding letter concerning Japanese petroleum purchases
subfiles.from: Charles Edison, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Forwards confidential Standard Oil correspondence about Japanese efforts to secure petroleum supplies.
subfiles.summary: The Navy Department sends the State Department a copy of E. J. Sadler's letter and a confidential communication from a Standard-Vacuum employee. It judges the information sufficiently relevant to State Department interests to warrant confidential transmission.

subfiles.title: E. J. Sadler to Admiral H. R. Stark on Japanese oil-supply efforts
subfiles.about: Reports that Japan was seeking assurances of increased petroleum supplies from the Dutch East Indies in anticipation of possible American restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Sadler explains that H. A. van Karnebeek's confidential report indicates Japanese pressure on the Dutch government for greater oil supplies. He identifies both the younger van Karnebeek's industry position and his father's high standing in Dutch public life to establish the source's credibility. A duplicate is supplied in case Stark wishes to forward the material to another department.

subfiles.title: O. S. Walden to E. J. Sadler forwarding the van Karnebeek report
subfiles.about: Forwards a copy of van Karnebeek's confidential April 1 report and describes the company's intended response to Japanese approaches.
subfiles.summary: Walden states that the report reached The Hague through the Dutch Department of Economic Affairs. He says the Hague office would keep negotiations open but consult Standard-Vacuum before allocating additional output, and asks to be informed of developments in New York.

subfiles.title: H. F. Prioleau to O. S. Walden on handling Japanese approaches
subfiles.from: H. F. Prioleau, Nederlandsche Koloniale Petroleum Maatschappij
subfiles.about: Transmits van Karnebeek's report and outlines how the Hague office would handle inquiries about increased petroleum allocations.
subfiles.summary: Prioleau reports that the confidential letter arrived through a Dutch government pouch at the Department of Economic Affairs' instigation. The company has not yet been approached, but would coordinate any possible allocation with Standard-Vacuum and requests reciprocal notice of developments.

subfiles.title: H. A. van Karnebeek report on Dutch East Indies oil exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports confidential Dutch East Indies government discussions of possible Japanese demands for increased oil exports following an American embargo.
subfiles.summary: Van Hoogstraaten asked petroleum-company representatives to keep possible Japanese negotiations open and to inform the government of any requests for increased shipments. Van Karnebeek recounts Dutch concern about avoiding both conflict with the United States and serious offense to Japan, while noting Japanese attempts to obtain oil lands. Current exports to Japan were about eight percent of company production, but participants believed the entire Indies output might barely cover Japanese needs if American oil were cut off, potentially prompting Japan to seize oil ports.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to the Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Navy's confidential transmission of E. J. Sadler's letter and enclosures.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State formally acknowledges Secretary Edison’s May 3 communication. The note identifies Sadler as a Standard Oil vice president and confirms receipt of all enclosed confidential correspondence.

subfiles.title: Harry B. Price to Joseph C. Green on Chinese-American contributions
subfiles.about: Requests guidance on accepting contributions and assistance from American citizens of Chinese ancestry.
subfiles.summary: Price reports a $1,500 contribution from Walter C. James and asks whether gifts from American-born members of Chinese communities present any legal problem. He emphasizes that such support forms only a small part of the Committee's income and carries no effort to control its policies. He also describes Lin Yutang's independent appeal to American readers and encloses that appeal, Price's reply to James, and a report on the Committee's program.

subfiles.title: Lin Yutang appeal supporting non-participation in Japanese aggression
subfiles.about: Appeals for financial and public support for the American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression.
subfiles.summary: Lin argues that American trade was indispensable to Japan's continued war in China and that the United States therefore had to choose between aiding Japan commercially and assisting China through trade restrictions. Because the Committee was an entirely American organization, he asks American readers to support it with cooperation and funds.

subfiles.title: Harry B. Price to Walter C. James on his contribution
subfiles.about: Thanks James for his donation while asking that Chinese-American support be channeled through American-born citizens and other Americans.
subfiles.summary: Price welcomes James's contribution during a financial crisis and appreciates his outreach to Chinese-American communities. He stresses the need to protect the Committee's claim that it was wholly American in support and control and free of foreign subsidy. He also reports cautious optimism about congressional action on war exports to Japan and promises the booklet “Shall America Stop Arming Japan?”

subfiles.title: Progress and Program of the American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: Reviews the Committee's organization, advocacy, finances, public-opinion work, and proposed program through June 1940.
subfiles.summary: The report traces the Committee's growth since 1938 and its campaign to end American credits and war-material exports that supported Japanese operations in China. It describes national and local organizing, publications, mailings, speakers, press and radio work, government contacts, and evidence of growing support for trade restrictions. Audited and interim statements document income, expenses, outstanding obligations, and a net deficit. A proposed twenty-week program calls for expanded publicity, mailings, Washington work, and special projects requiring more than $55,000 in special contributions.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Harry B. Price's report on Committee activities
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Price's April 23 letter about the American Committee's activities.
subfiles.summary: The Department briefly acknowledges receipt of Price's correspondence and the accompanying information. It offers no substantive ruling on the contribution questions raised in the original letter.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs draft response to Roger S. Greene
subfiles.about: Recommends acknowledging Greene's letter and assuring him that the Department welcomes informed public opinion.
subfiles.summary: The division proposes a reply to Greene's April 29 inquiry about directing embargo-related views to the State Department. Its draft says the Department welcomes and carefully considers thoughtful opinions on all aspects of foreign relations.

subfiles.title: Roger S. Greene to Charles W. Yost on responsibility for embargo policy
subfiles.about: Asks whether public pressure for restrictions on war-material exports to Japan should principally be directed to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Greene cites Yost's statement to Professor William Ernest Hocking that existing law did not authorize the proposed embargo. Noting Senator Pittman's report that Senate action had been postponed at the Secretary of State's request, Greene asks whether the public should address its views mainly to the Department. He argues that congressional reliance on executive leadership in foreign policy should be encouraged.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Roger S. Greene
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Assures Greene that the Department welcomes thoughtful expressions of opinion about war-material shipments and foreign relations.
subfiles.summary: The reply acknowledges Greene's April 29 letter. It avoids commenting on the division of responsibility between Congress and the executive but affirms that the Department considers informed public views.

subfiles.title: Allen T. Treadway to Cordell Hull forwarding an embargo appeal
subfiles.about: Forwards J. Franklin Carter's letter urging an embargo on war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Representative Treadway sends Carter's May 6 appeal to the secretary of state for information and consideration. He invites Hull to respond on the subject at his convenience.

subfiles.title: J. Franklin Carter to Allen T. Treadway advocating statutory embargo authority
subfiles.about: Urges Congress to empower the president to embargo wartime supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Carter says the voluntary or “moral” embargo had failed to stop American merchants from supplying Japan. He calls for legal authority permitting a comprehensive embargo and criticizes congressional timidity toward aiding democracies against totalitarian powers.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull to Allen T. Treadway on the absence of embargo authority
subfiles.about: Explains that no existing statute authorized the embargo advocated by J. Franklin Carter.
subfiles.summary: Hull thanks Treadway for forwarding Carter's letter. He states that implementation of the proposed embargo would require new legislation and returns Carter's enclosure.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note to Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs official
subfiles.about: Agrees with Hornbeck's doubt while emphasizing the importance of the legal or policy basis for action against Japan.
subfiles.summary: The writer shares Hornbeck's uncertainty about separating Japan's war economy from its normal economy. Nevertheless, the note stresses that the basis invoked for any American action against Japan remains important.

subfiles.title: Stanley K. Hornbeck note on Japan's war and civilian industries
subfiles.about: Questions whether Japan's war industry could be impaired without also injuring its normal industry.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck expresses doubt that trade restrictions could embarrass Japan's war production while sparing ordinary economic activity. The observation frames the practical difficulty addressed in the accompanying quota analyses.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs covering memorandum on export-quota feasibility
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Jones and Ballantine studies and concludes that a disguised export-quota plan aimed at Japan was infeasible.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum explains that officials studied whether quotas based on an earlier trade period could reduce exports to Japan while preserving shipments to Britain, France, and Canada. The study rejected that technique as impractical. It recommends retaining the alternative idea of limiting Japanese imports to pre-hostilities levels on the ground that later increases supported aggression in China.

subfiles.title: Joseph W. Ballantine comment on historical quota bases
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs colleagues
subfiles.about: Assesses whether 1909–1918 trade averages could support quotas restricting Japanese purchases.
subfiles.summary: Ballantine observes that a 1909–1918 base might sharply restrict Japanese crude oil, gasoline, and copper purchases without reducing exports to France, Canada, or the United Kingdom. He nevertheless concurs with Jones that country quotas would carry serious disadvantages. Because the proposed base included the First World War's unusually high Allied demand, its anti-Japanese purpose would be especially transparent.

subfiles.title: Jones memorandum and statistical annex on discriminatory export quotas
subfiles.from: Mr. Jones, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Analyzes whether general export quotas could covertly restrict strategic exports to Japan without reducing trade with Britain, France, and Canada.
subfiles.summary: Jones argues that any quota designed to reduce Japanese purchases while preserving other countries' trade would be recognizably discriminatory and would require a cumbersome licensing and allocation system. He finds little credible domestic-defense or conservation justification, though limiting Japan to pre-1937 levels could be defended as withholding materials used for aggression in China. Commodity analysis suggests limited possibilities for copper, gasoline, and some steel semimanufactures, but not for most petroleum products, machinery, automobiles, or scrap without harming other markets. Annexed tables compare United States exports of automobiles, petroleum products, copper, scrap, steel, and machinery to selected countries from 1920 through 1938.
